clue.text: As old Marley was to begin a favorite Carol?

definitions.text: As old Marley was to begin a favorite Carol?

parts.words: As old Marley was to begin a favorite Carol?
parts.note: Dickens opens A Christmas Carol by saying Jacob Marley was dead, to begin with, as dead as a certain piece of door hardware

explanation.walkthrough: 'Carol' looks like a woman's name, but it is Dickens's A Christmas Carol, whose first lines declare Marley as DEAD AS A DOORNAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means utterly and unmistakably lifeless, which is exactly how Dickens describes Scrooge's late partner.

clue.text: Help to get it up with a rigorously discriminating grade — it might be attached to a letter.

definitions.text: it might be attached to a letter

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting a word up means reading it from bottom to top, so the word for help is turned round

parts.note: to help is to aid
critical judgement discriminates rigorously between good and bad
a grade given to work is a mark

explanation.surface: Advice on how to push a student up to a demanding top grade, with a note pinned to a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'to get it up' means read from the bottom, so AID becomes DIA; 'grade' is meant as a score, not a school year.
explanation.definitionFit: Accents, cedillas and umlauts are signs fixed to a letter to show how it is sounded.

clue.text: The kind of man Gunga Din was might be of some aid.

definitions.note: the definition is adjectival in form; the answer is the person who is of some aid

indicators.note: the answer might be taken, by ear, for the phrase describing Gunga Din, so these words signal a sound-alike

parts.words: The kind of man Gunga Din was
parts.note: Kipling's poem ends 'You're a better man than I am, Gunga Din!', so he was a better man, said aloud as one word

explanation.surface: A remark on Kipling's heroic water-carrier and the help he gave the troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' signals a sound-alike: Kipling's poem ends 'You're a better man than I am, Gunga Din!', and 'a better' said aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An abettor is a helper or supporter, someone who gives aid, usually to a wrongdoer.

clue.text: It might be for gold.

parts.note: gold is traditionally tested with nitric acid, which leaves real gold untouched while base metals react

explanation.walkthrough: 'for gold' suggests a prize, but it is an assay: the original ACID TEST was dabbing nitric acid on metal to prove it gold.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase now means any decisive trial of worth, from the old assay check for genuine gold.

clue.text: Tools about which things might 11.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: chopping implements, the plural of axe
second meaning: 11 is ROTATE, and lines about which bodies spin are the plural of axis

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference to 11 brings in ROTATE; one spelling serves as the plural of both axe and axis.
explanation.definitionFit: Woodcutters' blades and the lines that spinning bodies turn around share the same plural spelling.

clue.text: Early and late, one isn't this.

definitions.text: Early and late, one isn't this.

parts.words: Early and late, one isn't this.
parts.note: someone arriving early, or arriving late, is in either case not arriving at the appointed time

explanation.walkthrough: 'Early and late' reads like 'from dawn to dusk', but it means arriving too early or too late, neither of which is punctual.
explanation.definitionFit: Being punctual means arriving at the planned time, neither before it nor after it.

clue.text: They might 11 with spit.

parts.note: 11 is ROTATE, and a spit is the skewer on which meat is turned over a fire

explanation.walkthrough: 'spit' suggests saliva, but it is the cooking skewer, which turns joints of meat as they cook.
explanation.definitionFit: Joints of meat cooked over a fire, often turned on a skewer, are the things meant.

clue.text: Exceeding all others in past history.

definitions.text: Exceeding all others in past history.

parts.words: Exceeding all others in past history.
parts.note: a record that beats every previous one ever set is the best of every era

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase describes a record or high that beats everything before it, as in an all-time high.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective is used of a record unsurpassed at any point up to now, such as a peak in prices.

clue.text: Drop down on the target.

parts.note: a shooter who drops the aim lower on the target is literally lowering the rifle's sights

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally it is a marksman's adjustment; the idiom means settling for a less ambitious goal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to reduce one's ambitions, from aiming a gun at a lower point.

clue.text: Similar to a mimic?

parts.note: to ape is to mimic, and an ape is a copycat
like means similar to

explanation.surface: A query about whether something resembles an impersonator.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces go in answer order, the copycat word first and the word for similar to after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Resembling a monkey or ape, the proverbial imitator, in looks or behaviour.

clue.text: One doesn't reputedly make a summer drink this way.

definitions.text: One doesn't reputedly make a summer
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the bird of the proverb 'one ... does not make a summer'
second meaning: to gulp liquid down the throat

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb warns that one migrating bird arriving does not prove summer has come.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the migratory bird of the proverb and the act of taking a drink down the gullet.

clue.text: To tear to pieces in turn?

indicators.note: tearing something to pieces breaks it up, so the letters of the two words before are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to rip something apart, taking turns to do it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to pieces' rearranges the six letters of TO TEAR; 'in' is a link, and the question mark admits the stretch of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To rotate is to turn round, or to take turns in a fixed sequence.

clue.text: Snow-bound writer.

parts.note: Snow-Bound is the title of a long 1866 winter idyll by a New England Quaker poet, not a writer stuck in drifts

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an author trapped by a blizzard, but Snow-Bound (1866) is Whittier's best-known poem.
explanation.definitionFit: John Greenleaf Whittier, the New England Quaker poet, wrote the idyll titled Snow-Bound.

clue.text: Does it involve having courage enough to do away with investment? Things stand out in it.

definitions.text: Does it involve having courage enough to do away with investment?
definitions.meaning: first meaning, whimsically: being bold enough to win relief from an investment, read as the two words of the phrase
second meaning: carving in which figures project strongly, so they stand out sharply

explanation.walkthrough: The first half splits the phrase into 'bold', having courage, and 'relief', freedom from a burden such as an investment.
explanation.definitionFit: In sculpture and figuratively, the phrase describes forms projecting strongly so they are vividly prominent.

clue.text: They might be crossed at entrances.

definitions.text: They might be crossed at entrances.

parts.words: They might be crossed at entrances.
parts.note: a doorsill is stepped over on going into a building

explanation.walkthrough: 'crossed' suggests something thwarted or marked with a cross, but here it is simply stepped over at a doorway.
explanation.definitionFit: The strip of wood or stone at the foot of a doorway, stepped over on entering a room.

clue.text: Have an inclination to be other than fat?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to tilt or incline
second meaning: the adjective for meat or bodies without fat, here read as a state one might be

explanation.walkthrough: One word serves as the verb for tilting and the adjective for slim or without fat.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to incline at an angle and thin or without surplus flesh.

clue.text: Getting even?

parts.note: read not as taking revenge but as making a surface flat and smooth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting even' suggests revenge; the question mark points to the literal sense of making something flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Making a surface flat and smooth, the American spelling with one L.

clue.text: 24 down obviously makes money!

indicators.note: the writer's name obviously makes, by rearrangement, a new word, so the letters of 24 down are reshuffled

parts.note: 24 down is the writer Sholem Asch

explanation.surface: A wry remark that a famous author clearly earns a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'obviously makes' says the four letters of 24 down's name ASCH, shuffled, plainly give the word for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Cash is ready money in coins and notes.

clue.text: Attila was one of God, but beat.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Attila the Hun was called the ... of God
second meaning: to whip or flog

explanation.walkthrough: Attila the Hun's title was the Scourge of God; the same word is a verb for flogging.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a whip, or a figure who punishes as one, and the verb to flog with it.

clue.text: They couldn't have more than nine commandments left to break!

definitions.text: They couldn't have more than nine commandments left to break!

parts.words: They couldn't have more than nine commandments left to break!
parts.note: people who have already broken the commandment against committing one particular sin have only nine of the ten left

explanation.walkthrough: The seventh of the Ten Commandments forbids adultery, so these offenders have already broken one, leaving nine.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who have committed adultery have broken the seventh commandment of the ten.

clue.text: They sang about her as being dear and sweet.

definitions.text: They sang about her as being dear and sweet.

parts.words: They sang about her as being dear and sweet.
parts.note: an old American parlour song names its heroine in a chorus calling her both sweet and dear

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the girl of the nineteenth-century parlour song 'Sweet Evelina', whose chorus runs 'Sweet Evelina, dear Evelina'.
explanation.definitionFit: Evelina is the sweetheart celebrated in the song 'Sweet Evelina'.

clue.text: Miss Novak has on nothing but a loose robe!

parts.note: the film actress Kim Novak
taken as written
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A gossip item: the film star is wearing just a loose wrap.
explanation.walkthrough: Kim Novak was the star of Vertigo; 'has' and 'but' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A Japanese garment, a long wide-sleeved robe tied with a sash.

clue.text: Treated like a king.

parts.note: the lion is the king of beasts, so being treated like one is being made a lion of

explanation.walkthrough: The king is the lion, king of the beasts, so to be treated like one is to be lionized.
explanation.definitionFit: Being lionized means being fêted as a celebrity, given lavish attention and admiration.

clue.text: Genus of the carrot and hemlock family as an ingredient of Rose's Elixir.

definitions.text: Genus of the carrot and hemlock family

indicators.note: an ingredient sits inside a mixture, so the answer lies within the letters of the next words

parts.note: the six letters run across the join of the two words, the end of Rose's and the start of Elixir

explanation.surface: A botanical recipe: a plant genus listed among the contents of a herbal tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as an ingredient of' puts the answer inside the letters of roSES ELIxir.
explanation.definitionFit: Seseli is a botanical genus of umbellifers, the plant family that includes carrots and hemlock.

clue.text: This writer sounds as though he'd either have to serve at court or be burnt!

indicators.note: the name, said aloud, sounds like other words, so the clue signals a sound-alike

parts.note: what is left of something burnt is ash

explanation.surface: A wisecrack that an author's name dooms him to be a royal servant or go up in flames.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounds as though' signals a sound-alike: the novelist Sholem Asch's name is said like ASH, what burning leaves; read by its spelling it could also be ACE, a serve at court (a tennis serve the receiver cannot touch).
explanation.definitionFit: Sholem Asch was a Yiddish-language novelist and playwright, author of The Nazarene.

clue.text: Going by what you already know, this ill-fitting pair took Rio by storm.

definitions.text: Going by what you already know

indicators.note: pieces that are ill-fitting are out of place, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mismatched couple storming Rio de Janeiro, as you might have guessed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ill-fitting' shuffles the letters of PAIR and RIO together; 'took ... by storm' only adds turbulence to the picture, and 'this' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A priori reasoning works from principles or knowledge held beforehand rather than from fresh observation.

clue.text: Not a nice word to apply to one in the building brotherhood!

definitions.text: Not a nice word to apply to one in the building brotherhood!

parts.words: Not a nice word to apply to one in the building brotherhood!
parts.note: the brothers who built houses of straw, sticks and bricks in the nursery tale were the three little pigs

explanation.walkthrough: 'building brotherhood' suggests a trade union or the Freemasons, but it is the three little pigs, each of whom built a house.
explanation.definitionFit: Swinish means like a pig, coarse or beastly, an insult for a person but literally true of a pig.

clue.text: A sign that someone is against the Wearing of the Green?

definitions.text: A sign that someone is against the Wearing of the Green?

parts.words: A sign that someone is against the Wearing of the Green?
parts.note: The Wearing of the Green is an Irish rebel ballad, but here the green being worn down is a lawn

explanation.walkthrough: 'The Wearing of the Green' is an Irish ballad about wearing the shamrock; here a notice protects a lawn from being worn by feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A notice telling people not to walk on a lawn is a sign against wear on the turf.
